a-servant-leadership.title: Agile mindset questions, servant leadership (purpose-people-process, characteristics, responsibilities) and the project manager's role in agile
a-servant-leadership.notes: Implementation strategy questions: how can the team act in an agile manner; what can it deliver quickly for early feedback; how can it be transparent; what work can be avoided to focus on high priorities; how can servant leadership help the team's goals? Servant leadership = leading through service to the team, understanding and addressing members' needs and development to enable the highest team performance; the servant leader facilitates the team's discovery and definition of agile and practises and radiates agile. Order of approach: purpose (define the 'why' with the team so they coalesce; optimise at project level, not person level), people (an environment where everyone can succeed and contributes across the work), process (don't seek the 'perfect' agile process - look for results; a cross-functional team delivering finished value often and reflecting on product and process is agile, whatever it calls its process). Characteristics: promoting self-awareness; listening; serving those on the team; helping people grow; coaching vs controlling; promoting safety, respect and trust; promoting others' energy and intelligence. Not unique to agile, but integrates well; facilitative leaders are more likely to become agile; growth mindset - belief that people can learn new skills. Responsibilities: manage relationships to build communication and coordination within the team and across the organisation, removing impediments and streamlining processes. Facilitate - shift from 'managing coordination' to 'facilitating collaboration'; help everyone do their best thinking; encourage participation, understanding and shared responsibility; expose bottlenecks within and between teams so teams resolve them; impartial bridge-builders and coaches rather than deciding for others. Remove organisational impediments - per the first Manifesto value, streamline processes (e.g., review documentation requirements with a department; challenge lengthy finance, CCB or audit processes; there's little point delivering every 2 weeks if release takes 6 or more weeks). Pave the way for others' contribution - team space with facilities, management agreement for one project at a time, stories with the product owner, regulatory process refinement with auditors, incremental budgeting with finance. Example responsibilities: educate stakeholders on why and how to be agile (value-based prioritisation, accountable empowered teams, quality from frequent reviews); support the team through mentoring, encouragement, training and career development ('we lead teams by standing behind them'), growing people even if they leave the team; help with technical PM activities such as quantitative risk analysis; celebrate successes and build bridges with external groups. Sidebar: interpersonal and emotional intelligence skills matter as much as technical skills - initiative, integrity, honesty, collaboration, humility, willingness to communicate - to adapt to changes. Role of the PM in agile: many frameworks don't address it and some think it unnecessary with self-organising teams, but pragmatic organisations find PMs add significant value with different responsibilities; 'the value of project managers is not in their position, but in their ability to make everyone else better'. PMs use servant leadership: the PMBOK definition stands, but in high-change projects there is more complexity than one person can manage; cross-functional teams coordinate their own work with the product owner; PMs shift from the centre to serving the team and management - coaching people who want help, fostering collaboration, aligning stakeholder needs, distributing responsibility to those with the knowledge.

a-team-composition.title: Agile team composition: team size, dedication, cross-functional roles (team member, product owner, team facilitator), generalising specialists, structures, multitasking cost, workspaces, silos
a-team-composition.notes: Agile optimises the flow of value (rapid feature delivery) rather than how people are 'utilised'; benefits: more collaboration, valuable work finished faster, far less waste from multitasking and re-establishing context. Agile teams: most effective size about three to nine members; ideally colocated; 100% dedicated; self-managing (members decide who does the work within the next period's scope); thrive with servant leadership; cross-functional teams collectively own the work and have all skills to deliver completed increments frequently; limiting WIP helps collaboration; collaborate by pairing, swarming and mobbing to avoid 'mini-waterfalls' (all requirements, then all design, then all build in a period - assumptions may prove invalid late and effort is wasted). Table 4-1 (verified): dedicated people -> increased focus and productivity; small team, fewer than ten people. Cross-functional team members -> develop and deliver often; deliver finished value as an independent team; integrate all work activities to deliver finished work; feedback from inside the team and from others such as the product owner. Colocation or ability to manage location challenges -> better communication; improved team dynamics; knowledge sharing; reduced cost of learning; able to commit to working with each other. Mixed team of generalists and specialists -> specialists give dedicated expertise, generalists flexibility; members often become generalising specialists. Stable work environment -> depend on each other to deliver; agreed approach to the work; simplified team cost calculations (run rate); preservation and expansion of intellectual capital. Table 4-2 roles: cross-functional team member (all skills needed for working product - e.g., designers, developers, testers; deliver potentially releasable product on a regular cadence; finished work fastest, higher quality, no external dependencies); product owner (guides product direction; ranks work by business value; works with the team daily giving feedback and setting direction; work small enough for an index card; works with stakeholders and customers; usually a business background with deep subject matter expertise, may draw on architects or product managers; needs training to manage flow; creates the backlog for and with the team; strong product ownership is a critical success factor - otherwise unvalued features waste effort); team facilitator (servant leader - may be called project manager, scrum master, project team lead, team coach or team facilitator; all agile teams need servant leadership; skills of facilitation, coaching and impediment removal take time; external coaches bring experience but weak relationships, internal coaches the reverse). Generalising specialists / T-shaped people: a focus specialty plus breadth across skills and strong collaboration, vs I-shaped people with depth but little breadth; reduce hand-offs and single-person constraints; a single person's throughput is irrelevant and focusing on it can create bottlenecks; the objective is flow efficiency (throughput of the whole team) rather than resource efficiency; small batch sizes promote teamwork; the product owner keeps the team on the highest-value work. Structures: colocated; distributed (cross-functional teams in different locations); dispersed (each member in a different place) - workable despite communication costs. Case: a US financial institution's follow-the-sun program (work handed off daily across time zones) started as one dispersed team with joint webcam standups and early-starting US roles, then split into five colocated, distributed cross-functional teams of developers and testers with central analysts and program-level product reviews. Case: the guide's own writing team was self-organising and incremental but not 100% dedicated, and tracked dispersion as a risk. Dedicated members: part-time (25% or 50%) members multitask and task-switch, lowering throughput and predictability; task switching costs 20%-40% productivity, rising exponentially with the number of tasks - someone split across two projects is effectively 20%-40% on each, not 50%, and makes more mistakes; temporarily assigned specialists (e.g., database administrators, research analysts) need explicit expectations about allocation and duration - part-time assignments create risk. Workspaces: a space to work together, see team state and collaborate; balance 'caves and common' - open collaborative areas plus quiet private spaces; distributed teams decide virtual vs physical mix, use document sharing and video tools, meet in person periodically to build trust; techniques: fishbowl window (long-lived video link opened all workday between locations) and remote pairing (shared screens with voice and video, accounting for time zones). Overcoming silos: start with foundational trust and a safe environment where everyone has an equal voice, plus the agile mindset; siloed reporting lines and differing metrics impede cross-functional teams - managers should focus on flow efficiency and team-based metrics and dedicate individuals to the team; first aim for a cross-functional team 100% dedicated to one team, even if only developers and testers communicating daily.

a-charter-practices.title: Delivering in agile: chartering the project and team, retrospectives, backlog preparation and refinement, daily standups, demonstrations, iteration planning, technical execution practices, troubleshooting (Table 5-1)
a-charter-practices.notes: Chartering: every project needs a project charter (why it matters, direction, objective); agile teams also need norms - a team charter. Minimum: project vision or purpose and clear working agreements. An agile project charter answers: why are we doing this (vision); who benefits and how; what does done mean for the project (release criteria); how will we work together (intended flow of work). A servant leader may facilitate. Team charter / social contract ideas: team values (sustainable pace, core hours); working agreements (definition of 'ready' to take in work, definition of 'done' to judge completeness, respecting the timebox, WIP limits); ground rules (one person talks at a time); group norms (how meeting times are treated). Retrospectives - the single most important practice: the team learns, improves and adapts its process (Manifesto principle 12); 2-week iterations prompt a demo and retrospective, but retrospect also when a release ships (however small), when more than a few weeks have passed, when the team seems stuck and work isn't flowing, or at any milestone. Allocate enough time to gather data, process it and decide experiments; not about blame; use qualitative (feelings) and quantitative (measurements) data to find root causes, design countermeasures and action plans; limit action items to the team's capacity - completing fewer improvements beats starting many; decide how to measure each improvement's outcome and validate it next period; a facilitator helps rank items and the team picks how many to take on. Backlog preparation: the backlog is the ordered list of all the team's work in story form; create only enough stories to understand the first release broadly and the next iteration; product owners (or a product owner value team) may produce a product roadmap showing the anticipated sequence of deliverables, replanned as the team delivers. Backlog refinement: in iteration-based agile the product owner and team refine stories for the next iteration mid-iteration so the team understands them and their relative size; continuum - just-in-time refinement in flow (take the next card and discuss it); a timeboxed 1-hour discussion mid-way through a 2-week iteration; several sessions when new to the product or domain; tip: impact mapping shows how the product fits together; the product owner leads, a servant leader can facilitate; the product owner may ask the team to spike a feature to understand risks; approaches: triads (developer, tester, business analyst/product owner) writing stories; presenting a concept the team splits into stories; exploring together so stories are small enough for a steady flow - aim to complete a story at least once a day; goal of no more than 1 hour per week refining - more suggests over-preparation or missing skills. Daily standups: micro-commitments, uncover problems, keep work flowing; timebox 15 minutes; walk the kanban or task board; anyone can facilitate. Iteration-based questions (round-robin): what did I complete since the last standup; what do I plan to complete before the next; what are my impediments (risks, problems)? Flow-based questions (board right to left): what do we need to do to advance this work; is anyone working on anything not on the board; what do we need to finish as a team; any bottlenecks or blockers? Antipatterns: turning into status meetings (common for teams from predictive backgrounds) and solving problems in the standup - log them in a parking lot and solve afterwards; encourage any team member, not the PM, to facilitate; decide consciously whether the work needs standups. Demonstrations/reviews: the team demonstrates working product; the product owner accepts or declines stories; iteration-based - all completed work at iteration end; flow-based - when a coherent set has accumulated; guideline: demonstrate working product at least every 2 weeks; frequent delivery of working product is fundamental to agility - a team that doesn't demo or release can't learn fast enough; invite the PMO and portfolio decision makers to see real progress. Iteration planning: capacity and story size differ per team; don't commit beyond capacity; reduced capacity (holidays, absences) means less planned work; teams cannot predict with certainty; smaller stories and finished product teach the team its capability; plan a little, deliver, learn, replan (source note: the text points to 'Section 4.10' for estimation examples, but no such section exists - measurements are in APG 5.4). Execution practices (largely from XP) to sustain speed with quality: continuous integration (frequently integrate work and retest the whole); test at all levels (system-level end-to-end, unit, integration where needed, smoke tests, chosen regression tests; strong preference for automation); acceptance test-driven development (ATDD - the team agrees acceptance criteria, creates tests, then writes just enough code and automated tests; non-software teams test chunks of value); test-driven and behaviour-driven development (TDD, BDD - write automated tests before the product to design and mistake-proof it; hardware uses simulations); spikes (timeboxed research or experiments for estimation, acceptance criteria, user flow, critical technical or functional learning). Iterations and increments create a cadence of delivery and feedback - demo, then retrospective to inspect and adapt. Troubleshooting (Table 5-1, verified): unclear purpose or mission -> chartering for purpose (vision, mission, mission tests); unclear working agreements -> chartering for alignment (values, principles, working agreements); unclear team context -> chartering for context (boundaries, committed assets, prospective analysis); unclear requirements -> help craft a product vision, a roadmap via specification by example, user story mapping and impact mapping, team-product owner clarification, progressive decomposition into a backlog; poor user experience -> UX design practices in the team involving users early and often; inaccurate estimation -> split stories smaller, relative estimation by the whole team, agile modelling or spiking; unclear work assignments or progress -> teach self-management, kanban boards, daily standup walking the board; team struggles with obstacles -> servant leader clears them, a coach if options are unknown, escalate what can't be removed; delays from insufficiently refined backlog items -> workshop stories with the product owner, a definition of ready, smaller stories; defects -> technical practices such as pair work, collective product ownership, pervasive testing (test-driven and automated) and a robust definition of done; work is not complete -> team defines a definition of done with acceptance criteria plus project release criteria; technical debt (degraded code quality) -> refactoring, agile modelling, pervasive testing, automated code quality analysis, definition of done.
